### **Introduction (5 mins)**

A Version Control System (VCS) is a tool used in software development and collaborative projects to track and manage changes to source code.

Git is the most widely used Distributed Version Control System (DVCS), which means every developer has a complete copy of the entire project repository, including its full history, on their own computer. It is highly efficient, supports branching and merging, and features a fast and decentralized workflow.

Git is the backbone of services like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket, making it a popular choice for developers worldwide.

So, what is the difference between Git and GitHub?

![][image1]  
*Illustration https\://www\.sprintzeal.com/blog/how-to-use-github*

The following table gives you a glimpse of the comparison between Git and GitHub:

| Git | GitHub |
| ----- | ----- |
| Git is a distributed version control system that tracks changes in the source code. | GitHub is a cloud-based Git repository hosting service that enhances collaboration and code management. |
| To manage versions of code and track changes locally. | To host Git repositories online and allow collaboration and version control via Git. |
| Git is a command-line tool installed locally on your machine. | GitHub is accessed via the web and requires no installation. |
| Maintained by the Linux community. | Maintained by Microsoft since 2018\. |
| Git focuses on version control and managing code changes. | GitHub focuses on hosting, collaboration, and project management. |

Below is an illustration demonstrating the importance of a Version Control System with Git and GitHub.![][image2]

Illustration [https\://medium.com/@karandeol2611/a-visual-guide-to-version-control-078d295354e7](https://medium.com/@karandeol2611/a-visual-guide-to-version-control-078d295354e7)

**Now, why use Git?** You might be wondering whether you really need to learn it. Is it necessary to learn Git, and in what situations or scenarios is it applied?

Git allows developers to manage project history, collaborate efficiently within teams, and revert to previous stable versions of code when needed. This is one of the key reasons why using Git makes the coding process more efficient. 

As you continue learning, you may discover additional reasons for its importance.

### **Module Learning Objectives (5 mins)**

After working on this module, you should be able to:

* Understand the importance and benefits of a version control system and the different git operations and terminologies  
* perform the basic git workflow: commit, push, and pull from a cloned remote repository   
* create, manage, and merge branches

#### **1.2.** **Understanding the Basic Git Workflow  (5 mins)**

The basic Git workflow involves synchronizing code between a local machine and a central remote repository (on GitHub, for example). This process is centered around **four stages,** *as illustrated below, with the first three stages being located in one’s local computer/ machine:*

![][image3]  
*Screenshot from [https\://www\.youtube.com/watch?v=e9lnsKot\_SQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e9lnsKot_SQ)*

Aside from the four different stages, the Git workflow also involves **four core operations:** cloning, committing, pushing, and pulling changes.

Below is a sample representation of the different Git operations and the stages or locations they affect in the Git workflow:

![][image4]  
*Screenshot from [https\://www\.youtube.com/watch?v=e9lnsKot\_SQ](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e9lnsKot_SQ)*

Here is a detailed comparison of the commands:

| Command  | Function | Scope |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `git add` | Adds changes from the working directory to the staging area, preparing them for the next commit. | Local |
| `git commit` | Records a snapshot of all staged changes in the local Git repository's history with a unique message. | Local |
| `git push` | Uploads local commits to a remote repository (e.g., GitHub, GitLab) so others can see them and for backup. | Local to Remote |
| `git pull` | Fetches changes from a remote repository and integrates (merges) them into the current local branch and working directory. | Remote to Local |
| `git clone` | Creates a complete, fresh local copy of an entire repository from a remote source for the first time. | Remote to Local (initial setup) |
| `git checkout` | Switches between different branches, commits, or restores a specific file to a previous state. | Local |

Here’s a 4-minute video of how Basic Git Workflow works. In this video, you are expected to gain a clearer understanding of the key concepts behind how Git works.

##### **Learning Resource 1: Video on [How Git Works](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=e9lnsKot_SQ)**

#### **1.3. Hands-On Activity of Git Workflow (50 mins)**

(Note: The student will be performing the Activity as guided or demonstrated by the Teacher \- Learning by Doing)

##### 1\. Let's **clone** a sample repository (gitHubRepo) created/hosted on GitHub. *(Check on how to create a repository in GitHub).*

In the screenshots below, you will see that the same repository from GitHub is cloned into a local repository (on one’s computer/machine), and the folder is opened in the Visual Studio Code editor.

##### ![][image5]

![][image6]

Cloning a repository is a specific form of downloading it from a platform like GitHub, but it includes the entire project history and version control metadata, unlike a simple download of a ZIP file. 

Cloning means creating a local, working copy of the repository that allows for full interaction with the version control system and collaboration with others.

Here’s a 2-minute Video that discusses the Process of how to clone a folder from your remote repository on GitHub to your computer (local Repository) using VS Code 

		**Learning resource:** Process for [Cloning a Repository from GitHub](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ILJ4dfOL7zs)

##### 2\. Now let's **stage** our Changes. First, let’s create our file, let's say **sample.html**, within our cloned repository folder *(Check how to create files within your Visual Studio Code editor conveniently).*

##### *![][image7]*

In the screenshot, the folder **GITHUBREPO**, which is a local clone of our GitHub repository, now has a file named **sample.html.** 

Now, notice the **indicator 'M'** beside the sample.html file. ‘M’ here means that the file was modified. Once we are done modifying our code, we can proceed to staging the modifications we made. To stage our changes, simply click the **\+** icon beside the file that was changed. As shown in the screenshot below.

![][image8]

Then, once our changes have been staged, we can proceed to “committing” the changes. 

##### 3\. **Commit** your stage changes. 

In the Source Control Panel, both the Stage icon **(+ sign** between the Undo button and M indicator**)** and the **Commit** button are visible.

![][image9]

To commit the changes, click the Commit button. REMEMBER to write a **Message** before clicking on the **Commit** button. The message should adequately describe what your newly committed changes are,  such as **“First Update”, or “Added a login form in homepage”**.

To deepen your understanding of Commit, here is a 7-minute video that includes a brief overview of the commit process.

	**Learning Resource:** Processes for [Committing Changes](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i_23KUAEtUM)

##### 4\. At this point, our changes are still in our cloned local repository **gitHubRepo**. To send our changes to our remote repository on GitHub, we use the push operation.

![][image10]

For us to be able to push our changes, we need to **publish the branch** first. You can think of a Git branch as our separate version of the main branch (the official project version in the remote repository); the changes we make in a branch do not automatically affect the main branch, hence the push operation. 

To publish a branch, we simply click on the **Cloud Icon** marked in the following screenshot. 

![][image11]

Then, other actions, like **Push**, will be available. Click the Push icon to push changes to the remote repository. Also, try hovering over all other icons to check their purpose.

![][image12]

After **pushing** (uploading), file **sample.html** with the message “**First Update**” should now be seen on GitHub as shown below.

![][image13]

##### 5\.  Finally, to update your local copy of a repository with the latest changes from the remote repository – including changes pushed by you or your teammates – you can use the pull command.

![][image14]

Let's try editing our code in GitHub and pulling our changes in VS Code Editor. Let’s say that on line 10 of our code, we will add a new paragraph. *(Check on how to edit your code on GitHub)*

![][image15]

As in local versions, changes in GitHub also need to be committed. This is done by clicking the “Commit changes” button in the upper-right corner of the window.

![][image16]

Before Pulling:					After Pulling:

Note that there might be conflicts that need to be resolved before successfully doing the operations. 

For example, a message that says **“Please clean your repository working tree before checkout”** means that you have uncommitted local changes (modified or untracked files) in your current directory that would be overwritten or lost if you were to switch branches or perform a pull operation. Git prevents the action to protect your work and avoid potential conflicts. 

The “working tree” is the actual directory on your file system where you edit files, which Git manages. 

VS Code Editor may suggest a solution, as shown in the example below.

![][image17]

#### **1.4. Branching and Merging**

At this point, we will learn Branching, which was mentioned earlier in this module. **Branching** is a core feature that enables developers to diverge from the main line of development (main branch) and work independently without affecting the main project.

Git branches enable different team members to work on separate features or experiments simultaneously without affecting the main codebase. For example, if you want to work on Feature A and your teammate wants to work on Feature B, VS Code provides tools for branch management so you can work on your respective tasks independently without affecting the main branch or other branches. It also supports Git worktrees for parallel development, and includes temporarily saving uncommitted changes (stash management).

**Merging** in Git is the process of combining the work from two or more separate branches into a single branch. It is the primary way developers integrate new features, bug fixes, or experimental code back into a main codebase once they are ready for production.

### **Closing/ Summary/ Key takeaways**

A well-structured Git workflow facilitates efficient collaboration, change tracking, and code quality maintenance for both individuals and teams.

Accuracy and productivity are increased when both Visual and Command-Line Tools (CLI) are used. Terminal Git offers full control and automation, and quick visual feedback is provided by Visual Studio Code Git tools (Explorer, tabs, gutter, minimap). Understanding the meaning and symbolism of the various indications helps to avoid unintentional or missing commits.

While you don't *technically* need GitHub to write code alone, it provides essential, free, and efficient tools for backup, organization, and professional growth.

In the next step, you will apply what you’ve learned in a group.

### **Glossary**

| diff editor (short for "difference editor") is a specialized text editing tool used to visualize, compare, and edit the differences between two versions of a file, or two different files entirely |
| :---- |
| **Minimap is** a small, on-screen graphical display—usually located in a corner—that provides a real-time overview of the immediate environment |
| **Octicons** is GitHub's own open-source icon set, designed specifically for its product interface.  |
| **Version Control System (VCS):** Git tracks every change made to your project files. You can go back to previous versions if any requirement arises. |
| **Distributed System:** Every developer has a complete local copy of the project, allowing for offline work and increased resilience. |
| **Git** is a tool that helps you manage changes to your code over time. It keeps track of every little change or update you make, so you can always look back at previous versions or undo mistakes if needed. |
| **Repositories:** A Git repository (or repo) is like a project's central hub where everything related to your work is stored and managed. |
| **Local Repository:** This is a copy of the repository that is stored on your computer. You can work on your project and make changes here. |
| **Remote Repository:** This is stored on a server, like GitHub, where you and others can share and work on a project. |
| **Commit:** Every time you make changes and save them in Git, these are called commits. The repository keeps track of all the commits you have made. |
| **Stage** In Git, the **staging area** (also known as the index) is a temporary "prep zone" where you review and format changes from your working directory before including them in the project's permanent history (a commit) |
| **Push:** The `git push` command is used to upload local repository content to a remote repository. Pushing is the process of transferring commits from your local repository to a remote repository.  |
| **Pull:** The git pull command is a core Git operation used to update your local copy of a repository with changes from a remote repository (like GitHub). |
| **Branches:** A repository allows you to create Branches and work on new features and fixes. For example, you can have a "main" branch for stable code and a "feature" branch for new features you're developing. |
| **Merging:** Once you are done with the branches you have made, you can merge those branches into the main branch. This adds the changes you have made in the rest of the project. |
| **Cloning** is a process of making a complete copy of a Git repository. It's like copying the entire project from a central location ( like a website) to your own computer. |
